§ 3MAJOR BIOGEOCHEMICAL CYCLES

CARBON CYCLE

  • The carbon cycle is a biogeochemical process where carbon is exchanged among the biosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and pedosphere. Green plants absorb carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, storing carbon. When plants die, they form fossil fuels. Animals obtain carbon by consuming plants and release it back through respiration and decomposition. Burning fossil fuels in industries releases stored carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, continuing the cycle.

WATER CYCLE (HYDROLOGICAL CYCLE)

  • The water cycle is a biogeochemical process where water moves continuously through the atmosphere, land, and oceans. Water evaporates from surfaces, forms clouds through condensation, and returns as precipitation. Some of it infiltrates the ground to recharge aquifers, while the rest runs off into water bodies. Plants also release water through transpiration. This cycle ensures the distribution and renewal of freshwater across ecosystems.

NITROGEN CYCLE

  • The nitrogen cycle involves the transformation and movement of nitrogen among the atmosphere, soil, and living organisms. Atmospheric nitrogen is fixed by lightning or nitrogen-fixing bacteria into usable forms like ammonia and nitrates. Plants absorb these compounds, which are passed through the food chain. Decomposition and excretion return nitrogen to the soil, while denitrifying bacteria release nitrogen gas back to the atmosphere, completing the cycle.

PHOSPHORUS CYCLE

  • The phosphorus cycle describes the movement of phosphorus through rocks, soil, water, and organisms. Unlike other cycles, it does not involve the atmosphere. Phosphorus is released from rocks by weathering and taken up by plants. Animals obtain it by eating plants. When organisms die or excrete waste, phosphorus returns to the soil and may eventually form sedimentary rock again. It is essential for DNA, RNA, and energy transfer in cells.

SULPHUR CYCLE

  • The sulphur cycle traces the movement of sulphur through the atmosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere. Sulphur is released into the air from volcanic eruptions, fossil fuel combustion, and decay of organic matter. It falls back to the earth via rain as sulphuric acid, is absorbed by plants, and then moves through the food web. Decomposition and microbial processes return sulphur to the soil and atmosphere, influencing both ecosystems and acid rain formation.
